<meta>continues from previous page</meta>applied with greasy wool. Olympias of Thebes <note>a famous midwife and writer on medicine from the 4th century BCE</note> added hyssop and nitre. The ash of a stag's horn is taken as a drink. The same is used for a laboring womb. Also, bull bile applied with two <term>obols</term> <gloss>small weights or coins</gloss> of opium is beneficial. It is helpful to fumigate the womb with the hair of a stag. They say that does, when they sense they are pregnant, swallow a small stone; if this is found in the excrement or in the womb (for it is found there too), it preserves the fetus when worn as an amulet. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb which are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. Concerning the pumice-like stone found in the wombs of cows in a similar way, we have already spoken in the section on the nature of cattle. Wolf fat applied softens the womb. It also prevails against pains of the womb even when harmful things have been applied. And it is beneficial if it is near a woman beginning to labor. Indeed, for one to come upon it is destructive <note>referring to a belief about the wolf's presence or influence</note>.

There is also great use of the hare for women. The dried lung, taken as a drink, aids the womb. The liver taken with Samian earth in water stops discharges. Rennet aids the afterbirth. They should avoid bathing the day before. Also, applied with saffron and leek juice on a fleece, it expels dead fetuses. If the womb of a hare is consumed in food, they believe they will conceive males. This is also achieved with their testicles and rennet. The fetus of a hare, removed from the womb, is said to bring back fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. But it is also healthy for the man to drink it before conception. Likewise, nine grains of its dung are given to a virgin so that her breasts remain firm forever. This is also done with rennet. For this reason, it is smeared with honey and blood where they do not want plucked hairs to grow back. 

For inflation of the womb, it is beneficial to apply the dung of a wild boar or a sow with oil. Dried flour of the same is more effective when sprinkled in a drink, as when a pregnant woman or one who has recently given birth is in pain. Sows' milk drunk with honeyed wine aids the labor of women. Drunk by itself, it refills the failing breasts of nursing mothers. If the breasts are smeared with the blood of a female pig, they grow less. If they are in pain, they are soothed by drinking donkey milk. Taken with added honey, it also aids their purgations. The aged fat of the same animal heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied on a fleece, it softens the hardness of the womb. Used by itself, whether fresh or aged and applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>a depilatory or hair-remover</gloss>. The aged spleen of the same animal applied with water causes an abundance of milk in the breasts. It also clears the face. Fumigation with donkey hoofs matures the fetus, so that it even evokes an abortion; it should not be used otherwise, because it kills a living fetus. If the fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to wonderfully settle discharges of blood. Also the ash of the same dung, which is also beneficial to the womb when applied. Horse foam applied for forty days before they are born stops the first hairs from growing. Likewise the ash of a stag's horn. It is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is aided by being washed with mare's milk. If a dead fetus is sensed, the spleen [of a horse] drunk in sweet water ejects it. Likewise, fumigation with the hoof or dry dung. Butter poured in stops a prolapsed womb. Bull bile mixed with oil of roses opens a hardened womb, with greasy wool and turpentine resin applied on the outside. They also say that a prolapsed womb is repressed and labor aided by fumigation with the dung of a male ox. Conception is aided by drinking cow's milk. 

It is certain that sterility can be caused by the trauma of childbirth. Olympias of Thebes affirms this is corrected by bull bile and the fat of serpents and verdigris with added honey, applied to the parts before intercourse. Also calf bile, if used during purgations or sprinkled on the womb during intercourse, both softens the hardness of the belly and diminishes discharges when the navel is pricked, and is generally beneficial to the womb. They set the measure of bile at one <term>denarius</term> <gloss>a weight of about 3.4 grams</gloss> weight, mixed with a third part of ammi <note>bishop's weed</note> and as much almond oil as appears sufficient; they apply this on wool. The bile of a male calf ground with half as much honey is kept for the womb. If they eat roasted calf meat with <term>aristolochia</term> <gloss>birthwort</gloss> around the time of conception, they are destined to bear males. Calf marrow boiled in wine and water with tallow is beneficial for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise fox fat, and the excrement of cats applied with resin and rose oil. They think fumigating the womb with a goat horn is most useful. The blood of wild goats with sea-palm <note>a type of seaweed or marine plant</note> removes hair. The bile of other goats, however, softens the callus of the womb when sprinkled on, and causes conception after purgation. It also acts as a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>depilatory</gloss> if it is kept applied for three days after the hairs are plucked. Midwives promise that a discharge, however immense, is stopped by drinking the urine of a goat, and if its dung is applied. The membrane of a kid, aged after the birth is produced and taken in wine, expels the afterbirth. They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a discharge of blood, rennet is drunk or applied with the seed of henbane. 

Aeschines <note>an ancient Greek physician, not the orator</note> says that if the loins of a woman are pricked with the blood of a black wild ox, a loathing for sex is produced. Likewise, a love-potion is made from the urine of a goat mixed with nard near the <term>fastigium</term> <gloss>the peak or extremity</gloss>. Nothing is more useful for infants than butter, by itself or with honey; particularly during teething and for the gums, and for ulcers of the mouth. A wolf's tooth worn as an amulet prevents the terrors of infants and diseases during teething. A wolf's skin provides the same. Indeed, their largest teeth, when tied to horses, are said to provide an untiring gallop. Diarrhea in infants is stopped by hare rennet applied to the breast. Donkey liver mixed with a little <term>panax</term> <gloss>all-heal</gloss> and dropped into the mouth protects infants from the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and other diseases. They prescribe this to be done for forty days. And a donkey skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that first fall from horses, when worn as an amulet, provide easy teething for infants. They are more effective if they have not touched the ground. Calf spleen is eaten in honey, and is applied for pain of the spleen. For running ulcers, it is used with honey. Calf spleen boiled in wine, pounded and applied, heals sores of the mouth. The brain of a goat passed through a gold ring before milk is given to infants is dropped into the mouth against the falling sickness and other diseases of infants. Goat dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat milk or the brain of a hare make teething easy. Cato thinks that sleep is produced by taking hare in food. The common people also believe it gives beauty to the body for nine days—a frivolous saying, yet there must be some reason beneath such a strong persuasion. The <term>Magi</term> <gloss>ancient Persian priests and magicians</gloss> say that sleep is induced by the bile of a sacrificed goat, provided it is smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow. The ash of a goat horn smeared on with myrtle oil inhibits sweat. Intercourse, however, is stimulated by applied wild boar bile. Likewise, swallowed pig marrow. Also donkey tallow mixed with the fat of a male goose. Likewise, from the mating of a horse, according to Virgil <note>likely referring to hippomanes, a substance used in love philters</note>.

<summary>This page catalogs numerous animal-based remedies for gynecological health, childbirth, and infant care, drawing on authorities like Olympias of Thebes and Cato. It covers treatments for womb ailments, fertility, teething, and pediatric epilepsy using substances ranging from butter and milk to bile and animal excrement.</summary>
<keywords>gynecology, childbirth, pediatric medicine, Olympias of Thebes, veterinary remedies, ancient pharmacology, epilepsy treatments, teething, hare rennet, donkey milk</keywords>
